title: Memory, GC & Low-Memory Handling
scopeHtml: Scope: per-app heap limits, ART garbage collection, bitmap and native memory, onTrimMemory, the low memory killer, leak mechanics at platform level, and OOM kinds. LeakCanary / profiler workflows belong to A6; process importance classes belong to the P2 chunk.

notes.title: App heap limit
notes.html:
What it is. Every app process gets a ceiling for its Java/Kotlin heap. Go past it and the runtime throws OutOfMemoryError and your app dies, even if the phone has gigabytes of free RAM. The ceiling is a per-app "allowance", not the phone's total memory.

Mechanism. The limit comes from system properties set per device build: dalvik.vm.heapstartsize (initial), dalvik.vm.heapgrowthlimit (normal cap), dalvik.vm.heapsize (cap with largeHeap). You read them at runtime:

val am = getSystemService(ActivityManager::class.java)
am.memoryClass          // MB: normal heap limit (heapgrowthlimit)
am.largeMemoryClass     // MB: limit when android:largeHeap="true"
Runtime.getRuntime().maxMemory()   // bytes: what your process may actually grow to

Typical numbers: 2012-era phones 48-64 MB, mid-range modern phones 256-512 MB for memoryClass, low-RAM (Go) devices as low as 64-128 MB. The value scales with screen density and RAM; never hard-code it. Android Go (<= 2 GB RAM, ActivityManager.isLowRamDevice()) has tighter limits.

Why a cap exists. Many apps live in RAM together; one greedy app would force the system to kill others. The cap also bounds GC pause cost.

What the ceiling does not include. Native allocations (NDK, bitmap pixel memory on API 26+), graphics buffers (GPU, textures), thread stacks and code are outside the Java heap limit but inside the process's real memory footprint and are what the low memory killer counts.

Real examples. Instagram and Pinterest size their image caches as a fraction of maxMemory(); Glide's MemorySizeCalculator uses memoryClass (about 0.4 of it, 0.33 on low-RAM devices for the bitmap pool plus cache; confirm in the source for your version). Google Maps keeps tile data mostly in native memory.

Real-life picture. Every hotel guest gets a fixed number of towels, regardless of how much is in the laundry. Ask for more than your quota and the hotel says no, even with a full cupboard.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying the limit equals free device RAM.
  • Hard-coding "16 MB / 64 MB" limits.
  • Ignoring that native and graphics memory count toward being killed even if the Java heap is fine.

notes.title: largeHeap
notes.html:
What it is. android:largeHeap="true" in <application> asks for the bigger cap (largeMemoryClass, maps to dalvik.vm.heapsize) instead of the normal one.

Mechanism. The process is started with a larger max for the Java heap. On many devices the large limit is 2 to 4 times the normal one, but it is a request, not a guarantee (the device's property decides), and it is ignored on some Go devices.

Costs.

  • GC pauses and collection time rise because the heap can grow before collection; a bigger heap means longer/more expensive full collections on some configurations.
  • The system treats big processes as better kill candidates when memory is tight; your app is killed in the background more often (the LMK works on RSS/oom_adj, not heap limit, so a larger footprint means a higher kill chance).
  • It hides leaks: the OOM is postponed, not prevented.

When it is legitimate. Photo or video editors, large document viewers, games with big in-memory assets (Snapseed-like editors, Lightroom Mobile, PDF readers). Even then, first try to reduce memory (downsampling, tiles, streaming).

Real examples. Heavy editing apps ship largeHeap with tiling. Google Photos relies on downsampled tiles, not a giant heap. Most social apps do not use it.

Real-life picture. Taking a bigger suitcase to the station does not make the train less crowded; it only means you take more space and the staff throw you off first when seats run out.

Common interview traps.

  • Using largeHeap as a fix for an OOM that is actually a leak.
  • Assuming it always helps; some devices return the same limit.
  • Ignoring that it raises background-kill probability.

notes.title: Memory categories
notes.html:
What it is. A process's memory is not one number. adb shell dumpsys meminfo <package> splits it into categories.

Category What it holds
Java Heap Objects allocated by Kotlin/Java (ART heap spaces)
Native Heap malloc/new from C/C++ code, many framework internals, bitmap pixels on API 26+ (see bitmap section)
Code Mapped dex/oat/vdex/so files, fonts
Stack Thread stacks (about 1 MB virtual per Java thread by default; native stacks too)
Graphics GL/Vulkan textures, display buffers, hardware bitmaps
Private Other / System Everything else, shared system mappings

Sample (shape only):

                   Pss  Private  Private
                 Total    Dirty    Clean
  Java Heap:     42000    41800        0
  Native Heap:   31000    30900        0
  Code:          18000     2000    11000
  Stack:           900      900        0
  Graphics:      27000    27000        0
  TOTAL PSS:    140000

Why it matters. "My app uses 300 MB but the Java heap is only 60 MB" is normal for graphics-heavy or native-heavy apps. The right profiler differs per category: Android Studio Memory Profiler (Java, native with native sampling on API 26+), Perfetto heap profiling for native (heapprofd), dumpsys gfxinfo / GPU tools for graphics.

Real examples. Maps and games show large Graphics and Native; WebView-heavy apps (hybrid apps) show big Native and "Other"; ML apps (TensorFlow Lite, ML Kit) show large Native and mapped model files.

Real-life picture. A kitchen bill with sections: ingredients, gas, staff, rent. A total hides which section ate the money.

Common interview traps.

  • Using only Java heap numbers to decide an app is "fine".
  • Counting shared code pages as private memory.
  • Forgetting thread stacks: hundreds of threads cost real memory.

notes.title: Bitmap memory
notes.html:
What it is. A decoded image takes width x height x bytes per pixel, no matter how small the file is. A 12 MP photo (4000x3000) as ARGB_8888 (4 bytes/pixel) = 48,000,000 bytes, about 46 MB, even if the JPEG was 3 MB.

Mechanism.

  • Pre API 11: pixels in native memory. API 11-25: pixels on the Java heap (counted toward heap cap, a major OOM source). API 26+: pixels back in native memory (allocated by NativeAllocationRegistry, freed when the Bitmap Java object is collected), which relieves the Java heap but still counts toward the process footprint and triggers GC pressure accounting.
  • Bitmap.Config.RGB_565 is 2 bytes/pixel (no alpha, banding), ALPHA_8 is 1 byte, RGBA_F16 is 8 bytes (wide colour), HARDWARE is GPU-only (see hardware bitmaps).

Defences.

  • Downsample: BitmapFactory.Options.inSampleSize (power of 2), or ImageDecoder.setTargetSize (API 28+). Decode to the size on screen, not the file size.
  • Reuse with inBitmap (API 11+, relaxed 19+) or Glide's BitmapPool.
  • Use a library: Glide, Coil, Picasso, Fresco (Fresco keeps pixels in ashmem/native on old Android).
  • Region decoding for huge images: BitmapRegionDecoder, SubsamplingScaleImageView.
  • Bitmap.recycle() is rarely needed on API 10+ but still useful for hardware-managed pools.
val opts = BitmapFactory.Options().apply { inJustDecodeBounds = true }
BitmapFactory.decodeFile(path, opts)                 // read size only
opts.inSampleSize = calculateInSampleSize(opts, reqW, reqH)
opts.inJustDecodeBounds = false
val bmp = BitmapFactory.decodeFile(path, opts)

Real examples. Instagram feed decodes at display size; WhatsApp creates thumbnails on send; Pinterest and Google Photos tile and downsample; Fresco was built by Facebook to move pixels off the Java heap on Android 4.x.

Real-life picture. A folded paper map weighs little in your bag, but unfolded it needs the whole table. File size is the folded map; decoded size is the table.

Common interview traps.

  • Estimating by file size instead of w x h x 4.
  • Saying pixels are always on the Java heap (true only for API 11-25).
  • Loading full-resolution into a 100 dp ImageView.
  • Not scaling thumbnails in lists.

notes.title: onTrimMemory
notes.html:
What it is. A callback the system calls on your app to say "memory is tight, please free what you can". It is a request, not a command.

Mechanism. ComponentCallbacks2.onTrimMemory(level) is delivered to Application, Activity, Service, ContentProvider, Fragment (you can also use registerComponentCallbacks). Levels you should handle (older TRIM_MEMORY_RUNNING_* are deprecated since API 34 because they are no longer sent):

Level Meaning
TRIM_MEMORY_UI_HIDDEN (20) Your UI is no longer visible; release UI-only resources. Fired when the app goes to the background.
TRIM_MEMORY_BACKGROUND (40) Process is in the LRU list, start of kill risk
TRIM_MEMORY_MODERATE (60) Middle of the LRU list
TRIM_MEMORY_COMPLETE (80) Next to be killed; free as much as possible

(TRIM_MEMORY_RUNNING_MODERATE/LOW/CRITICAL = 5/10/15 told a foreground app about pressure; deprecated in API 34.)

override fun onTrimMemory(level: Int) {
    super.onTrimMemory(level)
    if (level >= TRIM_MEMORY_UI_HIDDEN) imageCache.trimToSize(imageCache.size() / 2)
    if (level >= TRIM_MEMORY_COMPLETE) imageCache.evictAll()
}

Related. onLowMemory() (old, treat like TRIM_MEMORY_COMPLETE for foreground). Glide registers itself for onTrimMemory and clears its caches automatically. ActivityManager.getMyMemoryState gives your current trim level. ApplicationExitInfo.REASON_LOW_MEMORY (API 30) tells you after the fact that the LMK killed you.

What it cannot do. It is not delivered if the process is killed outright; it cannot guarantee you avoid kill. Freeing caches on UI_HIDDEN buys you a better LRU position (smaller footprint).

Real examples. Spotify trims album-art caches when backgrounded; Facebook/Instagram release feed bitmaps on UI_HIDDEN; Glide, Coil and Fresco hook trim callbacks.

Real-life picture. A librarian announcing "closing in 10 minutes, please return extra books": cooperating readers keep their seat on the list; others are asked to leave first.

Common interview traps.

  • Treating onTrimMemory as a guarantee you will be warned before being killed.
  • Using the RUNNING_* levels in new code.
  • Not trimming on UI_HIDDEN, the most useful level.
  • Doing slow work in onTrimMemory (it runs on the main thread).

notes.title: PSS RSS and USS in meminfo
notes.html:
What it is. Different ways of counting "how much memory does this process use", because processes share pages (Zygote's shared libraries and framework).

  • RSS (Resident Set Size): all pages of the process currently in RAM, including shared ones counted fully. Overcounts shared memory.
  • PSS (Proportional Set Size): private pages + shared pages divided by the number of processes sharing them. The fairest "share" measure and what dumpsys meminfo reports as "Pss Total".
  • USS (Unique Set Size): only pages that belong to this process alone (private). What would be freed if the process died. Private Dirty + Private Clean.
Shared library page, 4 KB, used by 4 processes:
  RSS: 4 KB in each (total 16 KB, overcounted)   PSS: 1 KB in each   USS: 0 KB (not unique)

Reading dumpsys meminfo. "Private Dirty" is memory only your process owns and cannot be re-read from disk, so it is the true cost. "Private Clean" can be dropped and reloaded from a file (code). "Swapped Dirty" matters on devices with ZRAM. adb shell dumpsys meminfo -a <pkg> shows Objects (Views, Activities, AppContexts, Binders): rising Activities count across rotations = leak. Programmatically: Debug.getMemoryInfo(info) gives getTotalPss(), getTotalPrivateDirty(), and getMemoryStats() map; /proc/<pid>/smaps_rollup gives the raw values.

Which to use. Compare PSS before/after for trends; use Private Dirty/USS for "what will killing this free"; the LMK works from oom_score_adj and RSS-like values, not PSS.

Real examples. Play Console "excessive memory" vitals and Firebase Performance memory metrics are PSS-like; Facebook publishes per-process PSS trends; LeakCanary uses heap dumps, not PSS.

Real-life picture. Five flatmates share a Netflix account: RSS says everyone pays the full price; PSS says one-fifth each; USS counts only what only you use.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying RSS and PSS are the same.
  • Comparing PSS across devices with different sharing profiles.
  • Summing the PSS of two processes of the same app and thinking it equals what the app costs when killed.

notes.title: ART garbage collection basics
notes.html:
What it is. The garbage collector (GC) frees objects nobody can reach any more. Think of it as the cleaning crew: it starts at known "roots" (static fields, thread stacks, JNI references) and marks everything reachable; the rest is trash.

Mechanism. ART's default collector since Android 8 (API 26) is Concurrent Copying (CC), a generational-less (until Android 10, later with generational CC in newer versions; confirm per release) compacting collector that runs mostly concurrently with the app, with short stop-the-world pauses (typically sub-millisecond to a few ms). Older ART used concurrent mark-sweep (CMS); Dalvik used stop-the-world mark-sweep with 10s-100s ms pauses.

What triggers a GC (visible in logcat as Background concurrent copying GC freed 12345(1MB) AllocSpace objects, ... paused 1.2ms total 25ms):

  • GC_FOR_ALLOC: allocation failed, must collect now (can jank the thread that allocates).
  • Concurrent: heap reached a threshold, runs in background.
  • Explicit: System.gc(); avoid it.
  • NativeAlloc: lots of native memory registered (bitmaps).
  • Heap growth, trim, and collector transitions (app backgrounded).

Reachability, not scope. An object is garbage only when no root chain reaches it. A static field holding an Activity keeps the Activity alive: that is a leak, not a GC bug. WeakReference, SoftReference change reachability; Cleaner/finalize delay reclamation (avoid finalizers; they run on FinalizerDaemon and can time out with TimeoutException ... FinalizerWatchdogDaemon).

Real examples. Instagram and WhatsApp scrolling jank traced in Perfetto/Systrace often shows HeapTaskDaemon and Background concurrent copying GC slices overlapping dropped frames; Jetpack Compose avoids allocation in hot paths for the same reason.

Real-life picture. A cleaner who starts from the front door and marks every room still connected to the building by an open door; locked-off, unreachable rooms get cleared out.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "GC frees objects not used". It frees unreachable objects.
  • Calling System.gc() as a fix.
  • Thinking the GC cannot cause jank today. GC_FOR_ALLOC and pause spikes still can on low-end devices.
  • Mixing Dalvik pause numbers with ART numbers.

notes.title: Allocation churn
notes.html:
What it is. Churn means creating lots of short-lived objects quickly. Each is cheap, but together they fill the young heap, force frequent GCs and steal CPU from your frames (16.6 ms at 60 Hz, 8.3 ms at 120 Hz).

Where it hides.

  • onDraw/draw allocating Paint, Rect, Path, String.format per frame.
  • Autoboxing: List<Int>, Map<Int, X> boxes each Int (up to 127 cached); use SparseArray/IntArray/ArrayMap.
  • Kotlin: lambdas that capture variables allocate a closure object per call (non-inline); for (i in 0..n) is free, but list.map { }.filter { }.forEach makes intermediate lists; Sequence or inline loops help.
  • String concatenation in loops, Regex creation in a hot function, toList() copies, Pair/Triple in tight loops.
  • Compose: unstable lambdas/objects created in composition on every recomposition.
  • JSON parsing building big temporary trees.

How to find it. Android Studio Memory Profiler "Record allocations" (Java/Kotlin allocation tracking), Perfetto with Java heap sampling, StrictMode, logcat GC lines showing frequent Alloc GCs, and macrobenchmark FrameTimingMetric. Look for a sawtooth heap graph with a short period.

Fixes. Hoist allocations out of hot code, reuse objects (pools: Pools.SimplePool, RecyclerView.RecycledViewPool), prefer primitives, mark lambdas inline, cache formatters, avoid per-bind allocations in RecyclerView.onBindViewHolder.

Real examples. Twitter/X and Instagram feed adapters, Google Maps drawing code and games all avoid per-frame allocation; Flutter-style and Skia code bases follow the same rule.

Real-life picture. Handing out a fresh paper cup for every sip: each cup is cheap, but the bin overflows and the cleaner interrupts the party every few minutes.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "small objects are free". Their GC cost is shared and shows up as jank.
  • Optimizing allocations in cold code.
  • Forgetting autoboxing in generic collections.
  • Believing escape analysis removes all garbage (ART's is limited).

notes.title: Low memory killer
notes.html:
What it is. When the whole phone runs short of RAM, the system kills background processes to free memory. The component is the LMK (Low Memory Killer); modern Android uses lmkd, a native userspace daemon (Android 9+, replacing the in-kernel LMK driver) that reads kernel signals (PSI, Pressure Stall Information, since Android 10 default).

Mechanism. Each process has an oom_score_adj set by ActivityManagerService based on importance: foreground 0, visible 100, perceptible 200, service ~500, cached/background 900-999. lmkd kills the process with the highest score (and largest memory) first when pressure thresholds are crossed. LRU order inside the cached range matters: the more recently used, the later you are killed.

oom_adj  FOREGROUND(0) < VISIBLE(100) < PERCEPTIBLE(200) < SERVICE(500) < CACHED(900+)  <- killed first

Consequences for your app. No onDestroy, no callback, no crash report (it is a SIGKILL). Detect it: ActivityManager.getHistoricalProcessExitReasons() (API 30) reports REASON_LOW_MEMORY; Crashlytics shows nothing; Play Console shows "background kills". After a kill, the system restores the back stack and recreates Activities from onSaveInstanceState: your app must survive process death (ViewModel SavedStateHandle, persisted drafts, WorkManager for jobs).

How to influence. Stay small in the background (trim on UI_HIDDEN), run a foreground service only when needed (service importance raises priority; Play restricts it), do not use largeHeap unnecessarily, avoid running multiple processes (each is a separate kill target and costs RAM).

Real examples. Chat apps (Telegram, WhatsApp) use foreground services or FCM to restart; music players (Spotify) use a foreground media service to stay alive; Xiaomi/Oppo aggressive killers add vendor-specific kills on top.

Real-life picture. A crowded cafe closing seats: the person who has been sitting idle the longest and with the biggest bags is asked to leave first.

Common interview traps.

  • Expecting a callback or log when LMK kills you.
  • Confusing LMK (system RAM) with OOM (your heap cap).
  • Forgetting that the foreground app can also be killed under extreme pressure.
  • Thinking START_STICKY guarantees survival.

notes.title: Leak mechanics
notes.html:
What it is. A memory leak in a garbage-collected language is an object you no longer need but that is still reachable, so the GC cannot free it. In Android the costly victims are Activity, Fragment, View and ViewModel-held contexts, because they pull huge object graphs (views, bitmaps) with them.

Mechanism. A path from a GC root to the leaked object. Typical root types: static fields, singletons, running threads, Handler messages in the main MessageQueue, registered listeners/callbacks, BroadcastReceivers, JNI global refs. The path "static -> singleton -> listener -> Activity" is a leak after the Activity is destroyed.

Detection.

  • LeakCanary (debug): watches destroyed Activities, Fragments, ViewModels and Views, waits 5 seconds, forces GC, if still alive dumps the hprof and shows the shortest strong-reference chain ("leak trace").
  • Android Studio Memory Profiler: heap dump, filter for Activity leaks.
  • dumpsys meminfo "Activities" count growing with rotation.
  • Production: Firebase/Crashlytics OOM rate and memory vitals; "OOM in onCreate" after long sessions.

Reading a leak trace. Start at the GC root (top), follow Leaking: NO to Leaking: YES boundary, and fix the first reference that is the problem (the link between the last "NO" and the first "YES").

Real examples. Square built LeakCanary after chasing exactly these leaks; Facebook has its own Memory Leak Detector in debug builds; WhatsApp and Instagram report catching Context leaks via static analysis plus LeakCanary in CI (instrumented tests with LeakAssertions).

Real-life picture. A hotel guest who checked out but whose name is still on a reservation list at reception: the room cannot be cleaned and rented because someone still "holds" it.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying leaks come from "forgetting to free memory" (there is no manual free).
  • Declaring a short-lived object a leak. A leak means it outlives its intended lifetime.
  • Ignoring Fragment view leaks (binding kept after onDestroyView).
  • Fixing symptoms (WeakReference everywhere) rather than the retention path.

notes.title: Common leak patterns
notes.html:
What it is. The few retention patterns that cause most Android leaks. All are "a longer-lived object holds a shorter-lived one".

// 1. Static / singleton holding Context
object Analytics { lateinit var ctx: Context }          // pass applicationContext instead

// 2. Non-static inner class / anonymous Handler or Runnable delayed on the main looper
handler.postDelayed({ textView.text = "x" }, 60_000)    // message -> Runnable -> this@Activity
// fix: removeCallbacksAndMessages(null) in onDestroy, or use lifecycleScope

// 3. Listener / callback never unregistered
locationManager.requestLocationUpdates(..., listener)   // forgot removeUpdates in onStop

// 4. Fragment view binding kept after onDestroyView
private var _binding: FragmentBinding? = null           // set to null in onDestroyView

// 5. Coroutine / RxJava subscription outliving the screen
GlobalScope.launch { repo.stream().collect { ui.update(it) } }   // use viewModelScope / repeatOnLifecycle

// 6. ViewModel holding a View / Activity Context
class VM(val activity: Activity) : ViewModel()          // ViewModel outlives Activity on rotation

Other classics: AsyncTask inner class (deprecated), BroadcastReceiver registered with Activity context but not unregistered, Dialog shown and not dismissed, static View caches, WebView not destroyed, Toast custom view holding Activity, RecyclerView adapters keeping a listener to the Activity after onDestroyView, LiveData.observeForever without removal, Lifecycle observers added to a longer-lived owner.

Spot-the-bug approach. For each field ask: "who holds it, and does that holder live longer than the screen?". Also check that thread/executor tasks capturing this end when the screen ends.

Real examples. Typical LeakCanary reports in the wild: InputMethodManager.mCurRootView, AudioManager leaks on old Android, TextLine, vendor-skin leaks (Samsung, Huawei); LeakCanary ships a list of "known library leaks" to ignore, and Google fixed several framework leaks over time.

Real-life picture. Leaving a sticky note with your phone number on a shared fridge: after you move away, people keep calling the old number.

Common interview traps.

  • Using WeakReference to cover up a bad lifecycle.
  • Thinking applicationContext is always safe (it cannot be used for theming or showing dialogs).
  • Forgetting Handler messages keep the Runnable alive until they run.
  • Not clearing binding in Fragments.

notes.title: Hardware bitmaps
notes.html:
What it is. Bitmap.Config.HARDWARE (API 26+) keeps the decoded pixels only in GPU memory (graphics memory), not in the Java or native heap. The CPU cannot read the pixels back, but drawing is faster and the app's heap and native footprint shrink.

Mechanism. Decode with ImageDecoder (setAllocator(ALLOCATOR_HARDWARE)) or BitmapFactory.Options.inPreferredConfig = HARDWARE. The bitmap is uploaded once to a GPU texture; each draw uses it directly without re-uploading. Pixel memory is shared via ashmem/AHardwareBuffer. Glide 4.x (DecodeFormat and Downsampler with HardwareConfigState) and Coil use them automatically when safe.

Limitations.

  • getPixel, copy, compress on a hardware bitmap throw IllegalStateException/return null; you can copy to software first (copy(ARGB_8888, ...)).
  • Cannot be used with Canvas software rendering, RenderScript, some Palette operations, or View.setDrawingCacheEnabled, and cannot be drawn into Bitmap-backed canvases (screenshots via PixelCopy).
  • Cannot be shared across to apps that need readable pixels (e.g. some image analysis).
  • File descriptor limit: each hardware bitmap uses a file descriptor in some versions (Android 8-9), so thousands of them crash with "too many open files"; Glide limits hardware bitmaps to images above a threshold and a fd budget (HardwareConfigState, around 700 FDs on Android O/P, confirm in the Glide source).
  • Bugs in some OEM GPU drivers; textures also limited by GL_MAX_TEXTURE_SIZE (often 4096 or 8192 px).

Rollout under live traffic. Gate by flag, enable for devices API 28+ first, avoid for images that need pixel access, keep the software fallback, watch Too many open files, Bitmap too large to be uploaded into a texture, and crash rate by device model in Crashlytics, and compare memory vitals (PSS) and frame times via Perfetto. Staged rollout with ability to switch off remotely.

Real examples. Glide enabled it by default for Android P+ on large images; Coil enables it by default on API 26+ when safe; Instagram-like feeds benefit from lower Java/native heap.

Real-life picture. Keeping a photo in a display frame on the wall instead of in your wallet: it looks good and costs no wallet space, but you cannot take a pencil and edit the pixels.

Common interview traps.

  • Using hardware bitmaps and then calling getPixel or Palette.
  • Believing they use zero memory; GPU memory still counts in Graphics.
  • Ignoring the file descriptor and texture size limits.
  • Enabling them for all images including huge ones that exceed texture limits.

notes.title: OOM kinds
notes.html:
What it is. "OutOfMemoryError" is not one error. The message says which resource ran out; the fix differs.

Message (typical) Meaning Usual fix
Failed to allocate a N byte allocation with M free bytes and K until OOM, target footprint ..., growth limit ... Java heap hit growthLimit Reduce object/bitmap retention, find leaks
... Bitmap / Failed to allocate ... bitmap on API 26+ native bitmap memory downsample, hardware bitmaps
pthread_create (1040KB stack) failed: Out of memory / java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: pthread_create ... failed Too many threads or virtual address space exhausted (esp. 32-bit processes, about 4 GB virtual) Use bounded thread pools, coroutines
Could not allocate JNI Env / Too many open files / EMFILE fd or JNI table exhaustion Close streams, cap hardware bitmaps
Throwing OutOfMemoryError "Failed to allocate ... until OOM, ... (large object)" Large object space fragmentation Avoid giant arrays; chunk
java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space but maxMemory far from used Often fragmentation or largeHeap mismatch (rare in CC) Profile
Native malloc failure / std::bad_alloc -> SIGABRT native heap or address space native profiling (heapprofd)

Mechanism. The Java OOM is thrown by ART when, after a full GC (and growth attempt), the allocation still does not fit under growthLimit. Thread OOM comes from pthread_create/mmap failure when the process runs out of virtual memory or hits RLIMIT/threads-max. 32-bit apps (ARMv7) have a ~3 GB usable address space; 64-bit lifts this, one reason Play requires 64-bit support.

Diagnosis. Crashlytics trace + custom keys (free memory, thread count Thread.getAllStackTraces().size, fd count from /proc/self/fd), dumpsys meminfo, heap dump on OOM (HeapDumpOnOutOfMemory is not available; use UncaughtExceptionHandler + Debug.dumpHprofData in debug builds, or LeakCanary), Perfetto.

Real examples. Large photo editors hit the large-object OOM when allocating full-size arrays; chat apps with unbounded Executors.newCachedThreadPool() hit pthread_create OOM during bursts; WebView-heavy apps hit native OOM.

Real-life picture. "The restaurant says no" could mean no tables, no plates, no waiters or no parking: the same refusal, different missing resource.

Common interview traps.

  • Assuming every OOM is a heap leak.
  • Not reading the message text.
  • Forgetting thread stacks and file descriptors as OOM sources.
  • Catching OutOfMemoryError and continuing as if nothing happened.

notes.title: Native memory
notes.html:
What it is. Memory allocated outside the Java heap: C/C++ malloc/new, bitmap pixels (API 26+), ByteBuffer.allocateDirect, WebView/Chromium, media codecs, SQLite caches, TensorFlow Lite models, mmaped files.

Mechanism. Allocated by bionic malloc (Scudo on modern Android; jemalloc earlier). The GC does not scan it, but Java wrappers register their native size using NativeAllocationRegistry (API 26+) so that the GC knows to run when native allocation grows; when the wrapper object is collected, a Cleaner frees the native block. A leak is typically a Java wrapper kept alive or a missing free/close().

Tools.

  • Android Studio Native Memory Profiler (API 26+; backed by heapprofd) records allocations with native stacks.
  • Perfetto heapprofd for long traces in the field-like conditions.
  • dumpsys meminfo "Native Heap" and /proc/pid/smaps.
  • libmemunreachable / adb shell am dumpheap -n <pid> for native heap dump (userdebug).
  • ASan / HWASan (hardware-assisted address sanitizer, ARM64, API 34 supported builds) for corruption bugs; GWP-ASan is on by default for some apps (API 31+) to catch use-after-free in the field.
  • StrictMode.detectLeakedClosableObjects() for closeable resources.

Production patterns. Native heap grows with the number of open images/pages (WebView), unclosed Cursor, direct ByteBuffers (freed only when the wrapper is GC'd, so a burst of direct buffers can exhaust native memory before a GC), long-lived ML interpreters, and OpenGL contexts. Crashes show as SIGSEGV/SIGABRT with a tombstone, not as a Java OOM, and Play Console reports as "native crash".

Real examples. Chrome/WebView apps and Zoom-style video apps carry large native footprints; Signal and WhatsApp's native crypto/media libraries; Google Photos' native image pipeline; ML Kit models.

Real-life picture. Storage in a rented warehouse next to the office: the office cleaner (GC) does not look inside it, so someone must remember to return the boxes.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing GC reclaims native memory by itself (only through Java wrapper lifecycle).
  • Looking only at the Java heap in the Memory Profiler.
  • Using allocateDirect in loops.
  • Forgetting to call close()/release() on native-backed objects (MediaCodec, Cursor, TypedArray.recycle).

notes.title: ART GC internals
notes.html:
What it is. A deeper look at how ART's collector is built so you can reason about pauses and heap shape.

Heap spaces.

  • Image space: pre-initialized boot classes (boot image), shared across processes via Zygote.
  • Zygote space: objects created by Zygote before fork; shared and never moved afterwards.
  • Allocation space (region space for CC): where your objects live, divided into regions; fast bump-pointer allocation with thread-local allocation buffers (TLABs).
  • Large Object Space (LOS): objects over 12 KB (arrays/strings) go here, not compacted individually (freelist or map-based).
  • Non-moving space: for objects that must not move.

Concurrent Copying (CC) collector. Marks reachable objects concurrently, then copies live objects from "from-space" regions to "to-space" regions, compacting memory and eliminating fragmentation. To let the app keep running while objects move, ART uses a read barrier (a small check on reference loads) so that a reference to a moved object is fixed lazily ("self-healing"). Short pauses happen only for root marking and phase flips. Since Android 10 CC can be generational (young generation collected more often; availability varies by release, confirm in AOSP docs); Android 12+ keeps tuning. Pre-8.0: CMS with a "sticky" partial collection and a mark stack, plus a card table and write barrier to find old-to-young pointers.

Write barrier / card table. Marks "dirty" regions when a reference is stored so GC need only rescan changed areas in partial collections.

Heap growth policy. Target utilization (~75% for foreground apps, per dalvik.vm.heaptargetutilization) decides when to grow; foreground apps get a more aggressive footprint; when moving to the background ART does a heap trim / compaction ("collector transition") to return memory to the OS and reduce fragmentation.

Reading GC log lines. Example: Background concurrent copying GC freed 18040(1103KB) AllocSpace objects, 3(60KB) LOS objects, 51% free, 6MB/12MB, paused 520us,300us total 23ms: freed counts, LOS freed, percent free, used/total heap, two pauses, total time. A repeating Alloc GC with large paused means allocation pressure.

Finalizers and references. FinalizerDaemon/ReferenceQueueDaemon handle finalizers and reference clearing; slow finalizers cause FinalizerWatchdogDaemon kills (TimeoutException: ... finalize() timed out after 10 seconds). Reference classes: strong, soft (cleared under memory pressure, behaviour is aggressive on ART, not a good cache), weak (cleared at next GC), phantom.

Real examples. Google's Android performance team's blog posts on CC and on generational GC; Perfetto traces in WhatsApp or Maps show HeapTaskDaemon threads running CC; Compose benchmarks compare allocation counts.

Real-life picture. A moving company relocating furniture room by room while people still live in the house, putting a little sticker (read barrier) on each moved item so you find its new place.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying ART still has Dalvik-style stop-the-world pauses of 100 ms.
  • Using SoftReference caches (ART clears them early).
  • Thinking the large object limit is configurable.
  • Relying on finalize() for cleanup.

notes.title: Leak diagnosis in production
notes.html:
What it is. A real incident flow: users report slow app and crashes after long sessions; Crashlytics shows OutOfMemoryError clustered around image decoding or onCreate, mostly on low-RAM devices. You can't attach a profiler to user phones.

Systematic approach.

  1. Quantify. Crashlytics/Play Vitals: OOM rate per version, per device RAM bucket, per screen. Custom keys: Runtime.maxMemory(), used heap, Activity count, thread count, session length, last screen.
  2. Reproduce. Soak test on a low-RAM emulator or device with adb shell dumpsys meminfo every N minutes while a script (Monkey, UI Automator, Maestro) cycles screens and rotates; watch Activities/ViewRootImpl counts and Private Dirty.
  3. Capture. Android Studio heap dump (Memory Profiler), or LeakCanary in a debug/QA build; in dogfood builds use LeakCanary's AppWatcher plus uploaded hprof (with PII care) or a "memory report" bundle.
  4. Read the retention path. Dominator tree, shortest path to GC roots, the "retained size" of the leaked Activity; group by class (many identical Bitmaps = cache issue, many Activity = leak, many Thread = thread leak).
  5. Fix and prove. Fix the root reference; add a LeakCanary instrumentation assertion in CI; compare before/after PSS/heap over the same script; roll out staged and watch the OOM rate in Crashlytics.
  6. Prevent. Lint rules, code review checklist for Context and listeners, StrictMode leak detectors, memory CI benchmark (Macrobenchmark with MemoryUsageMetric).

Pitfalls. Leak found only on release builds because R8/optimizations or SDK changes change retention; OOM messages that look like a leak but are a large single allocation; vendor-skin framework leaks that you cannot fix (use LeakCanary's ignore list).

Real examples. Teams at Square (LeakCanary), Facebook (OOM bucketing with heap-dump-on-OOM tooling on internal builds), and Uber (memory metrics per screen) follow this loop; Firebase Performance Monitoring has no heap profile so custom metrics are used.

Real-life picture. A detective following a muddy footprint trail: you do not guess the culprit; you follow the exact path from the scene back to who holds the key.

Common interview traps.

  • Starting with a fix before measuring.
  • Sending raw hprof files with user PII to servers.
  • Assuming the leak is in your code only; libraries and WebViews leak too.
  • Not distinguishing a slow growth leak from a one-off large allocation.

notes.title: In-memory image cache sizing
notes.html:
What it is. The design choice of how much RAM your image cache may use. Too small: constant reloads, jank and battery cost. Too large: OOM, LMK kills, slower GC.

Mechanism and numbers. Use an LruCache<String, Bitmap> sized in bytes (override sizeOf to bitmap.allocationByteCount), not entry count. Glide's default MemorySizeCalculator takes memoryClass x (0.4, or 0.33 on low-RAM) and sizes the bitmap pool and memory cache based on screen size (about 2-4 screens worth of pixels); Coil's MemoryCache default is a fraction of available memory (about 25% of memoryClass, confirm in Coil docs).

val maxKb = (Runtime.getRuntime().maxMemory() / 1024).toInt()
val cache = object : LruCache<String, Bitmap>(maxKb / 8) {          // 1/8 of heap
    override fun sizeOf(k: String, v: Bitmap) = v.allocationByteCount / 1024
}

Trade-offs.

  • Fraction of heap (1/8 to 1/4) plus a floor and ceiling; scale by isLowRamDevice().
  • Cache decoded size at the display size (thumbnails), not full resolution.
  • Two levels: memory (fast, small) over disk (larger, cheap). Disk cache hits decode again; skipping the memory cache for huge images is OK.
  • Shrink on onTrimMemory; separate pool for reuse (inBitmap) vs cache.
  • Test on 2 GB devices with other apps running.

Production incident pattern. After adding a heavier feed layout, OOM rises on 3 GB devices: cache was set to a fixed 100 MB; fix by deriving from memoryClass and by trimming on UI_HIDDEN.

Real examples. Glide/Coil/Picasso/Fresco defaults; Instagram and Pinterest run bigger caches on high-end devices and smaller on Go; Fresco uses "ashmem" or native bitmap pools and a multi-tier cache.

Real-life picture. Counter space in a kitchen: keep the most-used utensils on the counter (memory), the rest in the cupboard (disk); a counter too big blocks the cooks.

Common interview traps.

  • Counting entries instead of bytes.
  • Fixed sizes like "20 MB" regardless of device.
  • Caching full-size bitmaps for thumbnails.
  • Never clearing under onTrimMemory.

notes.title: Thread and native exhaustion
notes.html:
What it is. Post-incident theme: the process died not because of heap size but because it ran out of threads or file descriptors / native resources.

Mechanism. Each Java thread costs a stack (~1 MB virtual reserved, around 100-300 KB of it typically touched), kernel structures, and a slot toward /proc/sys/kernel/threads-max and per-process limits (ulimit -u, vendor limits often a few thousand, /proc/self/status shows Threads:). File descriptors are limited by RLIMIT_NOFILE (commonly 32768 soft on modern Android; older Android 1024; hardware bitmaps and sockets consume them). Signs: java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: pthread_create (1040KB stack) failed: Resource temporarily unavailable, Could not allocate JNI Env, Too many open files, EMFILE.

Typical root causes.

  • Executors.newCachedThreadPool() with unbounded bursts; a new Thread {} per request; libraries each making their own pools (OkHttp dispatcher, Glide executors, RxJava schedulers, analytics SDKs).
  • Blocked threads piling up (deadlock, network timeouts without limits) so each new request spawns more.
  • Leaked HandlerThreads, never quitSafely().
  • Sockets/files/cursors not closed; WebSocket reconnect loops creating a new client each time.
  • 32-bit address space exhaustion with many mapped files and threads.

Fix and prevention. Shared bounded pools (Dispatchers.IO caps at 64 threads by default), coroutines instead of threads, limitedParallelism, set timeouts, always use {} for Closeable, one OkHttpClient, enable StrictMode.detectLeakedClosableObjects/detectLeakedSqlLiteObjects. Add monitoring: log thread count and fd count (File("/proc/self/fd").list().size) as Crashlytics keys; alert above thresholds; dump thread stacks (Thread.getAllStackTraces()) when count > 300 in dogfood.

Real examples. Apps with chat sockets plus many image loads (WhatsApp, Telegram-style) enforce shared pools; Uber and Netflix describe thread-budget policies for their networking stacks; OkHttp's dispatcher defaults limit to 64 requests and 5 per host.

Real-life picture. A restaurant that hires a new waiter for every table and never sends them home: the kitchen door jams long before the money runs out.

Common interview traps.

  • Blaming heap when the message says pthread_create.
  • Creating a new OkHttpClient per request.
  • Assuming Dispatchers.IO is unlimited.
  • Forgetting file descriptors as an exhaustible resource.

notes.title: Low-RAM strategy
notes.html:
What it is. Design approach for apps that must also run on 1-2 GB Android Go devices where requirements are ambiguous ("make it work on low-end phones").

Clarify the requirement first. Which devices (RAM, API level, share of users), which flows, what "work" means (no crashes? 60 fps? start time?), and what features may be reduced. Without data you cannot trade off.

Tools and tactics.

  • Detect: ActivityManager.isLowRamDevice(), memoryClass, getMemoryInfo(info).totalMem/availMem/lowMemory, and device-class libraries like androidx.core / Jetpack DeviceClass/Google's Device Performance Class (media performance class API 31+).
  • Degrade gracefully: smaller image sizes and caches, RGB_565 for non-alpha thumbnails, no heavy animations, fewer prefetched pages, lighter ML models, disable background features, simpler video resolution.
  • Cut footprint: single process, avoid multidex-heavy libraries, drop unused SDKs, R8 shrink, split APKs/AAB (languages, ABIs), largeHeap off, lazy-load features (Play Feature Delivery).
  • Android Go edition: Lite app variants (Facebook Lite, Messenger Lite, Google Go, YouTube Go, Uber Lite) are separate builds with a tiny footprint; target <= 10-50 MB install and RAM budgets of tens of MB.
  • Verify: test on a real low-end device or an emulator with 1 GB, use Macrobenchmark and Perfetto, track Play Vitals by RAM bucket (device catalog segmentation in Play Console).

Real examples. Facebook Lite, Uber Lite, Twitter Lite (PWA) and Spotify Lite; WhatsApp tunes caches for 1 GB devices; Flipkart Lite is a PWA.

Real-life picture. Packing for a budget flight with a strict baggage limit: decide what you truly need before you start, and bring the light version of everything else.

Common interview traps.

  • Optimizing without an agreed device target.
  • Detecting low RAM with an API-level check.
  • Shipping the same bitmap sizes to every device.
  • Forgetting that the OS and other apps already consume most of 1 GB.

notes.title: Large payload memory
notes.html:
What it is. Cost/perf scenario: a large JSON/protobuf/file response (tens of MB) loaded into memory at once, causing OOM, GC churn and slow parsing.

Why it hurts. response.body.string() reads the whole body into a String (UTF-16: roughly 2 bytes per char on older ART, newer runtimes may store Latin-1 strings compactly; confirm for your API level). Then a Gson/Moshi tree creates more objects: peak memory can be 3 to 5 times the payload size (bytes + string + object graph). Large arrays go to the Large Object Space and fragment.

Fixes (in order of impact).

  1. Stream: Moshi/Gson JsonReader or kotlinx.serialization decodeToSequence over the BufferedSource; process item by item; write to Room in batches (@Transaction, 500-1000 rows).
  2. Paginate at the API (cursor/page size) and use Paging 3 with RemoteMediator.
  3. Download to disk (OkHttp sink, DownloadManager, WorkManager) and parse from the file or mmap.
  4. Compress (gzip/brotli, protobuf/flatbuffers for compact formats) and trim fields (sparse fieldsets, GraphQL).
  5. Avoid copies: ByteString/Buffer from Okio share segments; avoid readText(); use ByteBuffer slices.
  6. Move parsing to a background thread with bounded concurrency.
response.body!!.source().use { src ->
    JsonReader.of(src).use { r -> r.beginArray(); while (r.hasNext()) dao.insert(adapter.fromJson(r)!!); r.endArray() }
}

Real examples. Spotify/Netflix catalog syncs paginate; Google Maps downloads offline regions as files; Slack and WhatsApp history sync use incremental pages; Firebase/Firestore paginates by cursors.

Real-life picture. Drinking a lake through a straw versus pouring the lake into your cup: stream a bit at a time and put each sip away.

Common interview traps.

  • Counting only the payload size, not the peak (bytes + string + objects).
  • Parsing on the main thread.
  • Putting the whole result into one List and one transaction.
  • Forgetting to close the response body.

notes.title: Hardware bitmap rollout
notes.html:
What it is. The migration scenario: enabling hardware bitmaps across a live app with millions of users without regressions.

Plan.

  1. Audit pixel access: grep for getPixel, Palette.from(bitmap), bitmap.copy, Canvas(bitmap), bitmap.compress, PixelCopy, blur libraries, Bitmap.createBitmap(source...), screenshot/share features. These need software copies (copy(Bitmap.Config.ARGB_8888, false)) or must request disallowHardwareConfig() in Glide / allowHardware(false) in Coil for those requests.
  2. Check library versions: Glide 4.x and Coil enable it conditionally; custom transformations need software bitmaps.
  3. Flag it: Remote Config / feature flag, API 28+ first (more stable drivers), exclude known bad device models, keep per-request opt-out.
  4. Mind limits: file descriptors (hundreds per process on API 26-27), texture size limits (GL_MAX_TEXTURE_SIZE), huge images fall back to software.
  5. Measure: PSS/Java+native heap per screen before/after, frame time (Perfetto, FrameTimingMetric), OOM rate, startup, crash signatures like IllegalStateException: Software rendering doesn't support hardware bitmaps, Cannot copy hardware bitmap, Too many open files.
  6. Staged rollout: 1% to 5% to 25% to 100%, with a kill switch; segment by device brand and RAM.
  7. Clean up: remove obsolete bitmap-pool tricks that no longer apply.

Real examples. Glide's adoption story (hardware bitmaps enabled with fd budget logic), Coil's allowHardware default behaviour, and Google Photos-style apps with editors that keep a software path for editing.

Real-life picture. Moving a shop's goods to a glass display cabinet: customers see them better and your counter is free, but you must keep a back-room copy for the items people want to alter.

Common interview traps.

  • Flipping the global switch without auditing getPixel/software canvas users.
  • No kill switch.
  • Judging success only by average memory; crash and jank tails matter.
  • Ignoring OEM driver bugs.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Heap limit is a per-app cap (memoryClass), not free RAM; native, graphics and thread stacks are outside it but still count toward being killed.
  • largeHeap raises the cap but increases GC cost and kill risk; it hides leaks.
  • Break memory down by category in dumpsys meminfo; PSS shares, USS is unique, RSS overcounts.
  • Bitmap cost is width x height x bytes per pixel; pixels are on the Java heap API 11-25 and native on 26+; always downsample.
  • onTrimMemory(UI_HIDDEN) is the key callback; RUNNING_* levels are deprecated.
  • ART uses a concurrent copying collector with read barriers; churn and GC_FOR_ALLOC still cause jank; avoid System.gc() and finalizers.
  • LMK/lmkd kills cached processes by oom_score_adj with no callback; survive process death.
  • Leaks are reachability paths from GC roots; LeakCanary shows the path; common patterns: static Context, Handler, unregistered listeners, Fragment binding, long coroutines.
  • Hardware bitmaps save heap but forbid pixel access and consume file descriptors and texture limits.
  • Read OOM messages: heap, native, thread, fd and large-object OOMs have different fixes.
  • Size caches in bytes as a fraction of memoryClass, stream large payloads, and design low-RAM tiers from measured device data.

questions.promptHtml: Why does an Android app get an OutOfMemoryError when the phone still has gigabytes of free RAM? How do you find out your app's heap limit at runtime?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you know the Java heap is capped per app by the OS, independent of physical RAM. Juniors assume "OOM = phone out of memory".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Every app process gets a hard cap on its managed (ART) Java heap, set per device by system properties, not by free RAM. When the heap hits that cap and a GC can't free enough, ART throws OutOfMemoryError even if the device has plenty free. I read it with ActivityManager.getMemoryClass() (MB) or Runtime.getRuntime().maxMemory() (bytes). It is typically 128 to 512 MB on modern phones and much lower on old or low-RAM devices, so I never hardcode sizes.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The cap exists so one app cannot starve the system and so the low memory killer (LMK) has predictable processes to reclaim.

  • dalvik.vm.heapgrowthlimit is the normal cap. getMemoryClass() returns it in MB. Runtime.maxMemory() returns the same limit in bytes (without largeHeap).
  • dalvik.vm.heapsize is the larger cap used when the manifest sets android:largeHeap="true". getLargeMemoryClass() returns it.
  • dalvik.vm.heapstartsize, heapminfree, heapmaxfree, heaptargetutilization shape how the heap grows between start and cap. The heap does not start at the cap; it grows as the allocator needs and GC targets a utilization (default around 0.75 in AOSP).
  • Values are OEM and device specific. I have seen 48 to 64 MB on old low-end devices and 256 to 512 MB on current flagships. Treat any number I quote as "typical, verify on the device".
Physical RAM 8 GB (free: 3 GB)
 |
 +-- Process A (your app)  Java heap cap = 256 MB   <-- OOM here even though 3 GB are free
 +-- Process B             ...

Important: the cap applies to the Java heap only. Native allocations (malloc, and bitmap pixels from Android 8.0 / API 26) are not under this cap, but they are still under device-wide pressure and LMK.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val am = getSystemService(ActivityManager::class.java)
val classMb = am.memoryClass                       // heapgrowthlimit in MB
val largeMb = am.largeMemoryClass                  // heapsize in MB (needs largeHeap=true to use)
val maxBytes = Runtime.getRuntime().maxMemory()    // current cap in bytes
val used = Runtime.getRuntime().let { it.totalMemory() - it.freeMemory() }
val lowRam = am.isLowRamDevice                     // true on Android Go style devices
Log.d("MEM", "class=$classMb MB large=$largeMb MB max=${maxBytes shr 20} MB used=${used shr 20} MB lowRam=$lowRam")

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Sizing caches as "10% of device RAM". Size from memoryClass or maxMemory().
  • Believing largeHeap is a fix. It raises the Java cap only, and costs more GC work and more kill risk (see the largeHeap question).
  • Reading totalMemory() as "memory used". It is the current heap size; used = total - free.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does the cap also limit bitmap pixels? → Not since 8.0 (API 26): pixel data is in the native heap. Before that (3.0 to 7.1) pixels lived in the Java heap and counted.
  2. Is maxMemory() the same on every phone with the same RAM? → No. It depends on OEM properties and screen density; two 4 GB phones can differ by 2x.
  3. If the Java heap is under the cap, can the app still be killed for memory? → Yes. LMK kills by system-wide pressure and process importance, with no relation to your Java cap.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "heap limit is 256 MB, use largeHeap." Senior: names the properties, knows the cap is Java-only, sizes caches from memoryClass/isLowRamDevice, and separates "Java OOM" from "LMK kill" in crash telemetry.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A photo app hardcoded a 100 MB in-memory cache; fine on test flagships (cap 512 MB), instant OOMs on 192 MB devices.

questions.promptHtml: What does android:largeHeap="true" actually do, and when would you refuse to add it in a code review?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who treat it as a free OOM fix from people who understand it just moves the ceiling and has costs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: largeHeap asks the system to use the larger dalvik.vm.heapsize cap instead of heapgrowthlimit for my process's Java heap. It is a request, not a guarantee, and on many devices the two values are equal. The costs are longer GC cycles on a bigger heap and a larger footprint that makes my process a better LMK victim. I only accept it for apps with a genuinely huge working set, such as a photo or video editor, and only after profiling shows the memory is justified.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Without it: cap = getMemoryClass() MB. With it: cap = getLargeMemoryClass() MB.
  • It does not help native or graphics memory. Since API 26 bitmap pixels are native, so largeHeap does nothing for them.
  • Larger heap means each collection has more live objects to mark and more fragmentation to manage. Concurrent copying GC keeps pauses short, but total GC CPU time and allocation stalls rise.
  • A bigger resident footprint raises the chance LMK kills the process when the user is in another app. Result: slower relaunch (cold start) and lost in-memory state.
  • It masks leaks. A leak that would crash in 5 minutes under a 192 MB cap crashes in 15 under 512 MB, which is harder to reproduce and worse for debugging.
Normal:       |==== heapgrowthlimit (e.g. 256 MB) ====|
largeHeap:    |==== heapsize        (e.g. 512 MB)  ========|
              ^ OOM here without it                ^ OOM here with it

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
<application
    android:largeHeap="true"
    ... />
// Verify you actually got more
val am = getSystemService(ActivityManager::class.java)
Log.d("MEM", "normal=${am.memoryClass}MB large=${am.largeMemoryClass}MB max=${Runtime.getRuntime().maxMemory() shr 20}MB")

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Adding it as the first reaction to an OOM crash instead of taking a heap dump.
  • Assuming it applies to the whole process memory. Java heap only.
  • Testing on a device where memoryClass == largeMemoryClass, seeing no difference, and concluding it is harmless.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What would you do instead for a big image editor? → Tile or downsample, reuse bitmaps via a pool, decode with ImageDecoder.setTargetSize, keep pixels native/hardware, and process in strips.
  2. How can you tell the flag took effect? → Compare Runtime.maxMemory() against memoryClass.
  3. Can the OS ignore it? → Yes; it is a hint. Low-RAM devices may not have a larger value to offer.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "gives more memory, use it if OOM." Senior: explains the mechanism, side effects on GC and LMK, how it hides leaks, and proposes structural alternatives.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team shipped largeHeap to "fix" OOMs; the OOM rate fell 30% but cold-start rate rose and background kills doubled because the app was now the biggest cached process.

questions.promptHtml: Name the different kinds of memory an Android app process uses, and which of them are limited by the Java heap cap.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The most common memory confusion: people watch only the Java heap and miss native and graphics growth.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A process has the ART Java heap (my objects, capped), the native heap (malloc, C++ libraries, and bitmap pixels from 8.0), graphics memory (GPU textures, surface buffers, hardware bitmaps), code (mapped dex, oat/vdex, .so files), thread stacks, and other mmapped files. Only the Java heap has the per-app cap. The whole process is still subject to device pressure and LMK.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
dumpsys meminfo <pkg> reports these rows, which map directly to the categories:

Row What it is Capped by heap limit?
Java Heap ART managed objects (Kotlin/Java) Yes
Native Heap malloc/new, libc, NDK, bitmap pixels (API 26+), direct ByteBuffers No
Code mapped .dex/.oat/.vdex/.so/.jar No
Stack thread stacks No
Graphics GL/Vulkan buffers, textures, gralloc, hardware bitmaps No
Private Other ashmem/memfd, mapped fonts, misc No
System shared system memory attributed to you No

Typical healthy split for a mid-size app: Java 40 to 120 MB, Native 30 to 100 MB, Graphics 50 to 200 MB depending on screen size and image use. These are rough ranges, not limits.

The consequence: an app can have a 60 MB Java heap, 500 MB total PSS, and get LMK-killed, while its Java OOM dashboard is clean.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
adb shell dumpsys meminfo com.example.app
adb shell dumpsys meminfo -a com.example.app   # more detail
val mi = Debug.MemoryInfo()
Debug.getMemoryInfo(mi)
val stats = mi.memoryStats           // keys: summary.java-heap, summary.native-heap, summary.graphics, ...
Log.d("MEM", stats.toString())

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using Runtime.totalMemory() as the whole app footprint.
  • Blaming the Java heap for a growth that is really in Graphics (e.g., unbounded texture/bitmap use).
  • Treating "Native Heap" as C++ only; bitmap pixels from 8.0 are in there too.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where do hardware bitmaps show up? → In graphics memory, not Java or native heap.
  2. Why does Code memory matter? → Mapped file pages are shared and reclaimable, so they are cheap compared with anonymous dirty memory.
  3. Which category is the usual cause of "memory grows but Java heap flat"? → Native heap (direct buffers, JNI leaks, bitmaps) or Graphics.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Java heap and native heap." Senior: lists all categories, ties each to a meminfo row, and says which are capped and which can silently grow.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A video-thumbnail screen kept 4K frames as Bitmaps: Java heap flat at 70 MB, Native 700 MB, silent LMK kills, nothing in Crashlytics.

questions.promptHtml: How much memory does a decoded bitmap take, and where does that memory live? Why can a 200 KB JPEG blow up a low-end phone?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Bitmap sizing is the number one real-world memory topic. The math must be automatic.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Memory is width x height x bytes per pixel, independent of file size. ARGB_8888 is 4 bytes per pixel, so a 4000x3000 photo is 12,000,000 x 4 = 48,000,000 bytes, about 45.8 MiB, even if the JPEG file is 2 MB. From Android 8.0 the pixel buffer is in native memory (tracked so GC still reacts); on 3.0 to 7.1 it was in the Java heap. Drawable resources can also be scaled up by density at decode time.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Config sizes: ARGB_8888 = 4 B, RGB_565 = 2 B (no alpha), RGBA_F16 = 8 B, ALPHA_8 = 1 B, HARDWARE = GPU resident.
  • Compressed file size only matters for storage and network. Decoded size is what RAM pays.
  • Density scaling trap: a PNG put in drawable-mdpi and loaded on a 480 dpi (xxhdpi) device is scaled by 480/160 = 3 per axis, so memory grows 9x. A 1000x1000 mdpi image becomes 3000x3000 x 4 = 36,000,000 bytes (34.3 MiB). Put assets in the right bucket or drawable-nodpi, and use BitmapFactory.Options.inScaled=false if needed.
  • Where it lives:
    • API < 11: native. API 11 to 25: Java heap (so it counted toward the cap). API 26+: native heap via NativeAllocationRegistry, so allocation pressure still triggers GC.
  • Reduce by downsampling at decode: inSampleSize (powers of 2) or ImageDecoder.setTargetSize (API 28+), then load only the size the ImageView shows.
JPEG 2 MB on disk  --decode-->  12,000,000 px x 4 B = 45.8 MiB in RAM
display ImageView 360x270 only needs 97,200 px x 4 B = 0.37 MiB

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// API 28+: decode directly at target size
val src = ImageDecoder.createSource(file)
val bmp = ImageDecoder.decodeBitmap(src) { decoder, info, _ ->
    val scale = minOf(1f, 1080f / maxOf(info.size.width, info.size.height))
    decoder.setTargetSize((info.size.width * scale).toInt(), (info.size.height * scale).toInt())
}

// Pre-28 / BitmapFactory: two-pass with inSampleSize
val o = BitmapFactory.Options().apply { inJustDecodeBounds = true }
BitmapFactory.decodeFile(path, o)
o.inSampleSize = Integer.highestOneBit(maxOf(o.outWidth / 1080, 1))
o.inJustDecodeBounds = false
val small = BitmapFactory.decodeFile(path, o)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Estimating from file size.
  • Assets in drawable-mdpi only, upscaled on high density devices.
  • Calling recycle() out of habit; since 3.0 it rarely matters, and recycling a bitmap still on screen crashes ("Canvas: trying to use a recycled bitmap").

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does Bitmap.getAllocationByteCount() vs getByteCount() give? → Allocation count is the real buffer size (can exceed byte count when a bitmap was reused with a larger one); use it for cache accounting.
  2. Can you cut memory without lowering visible quality? → Use RGB_565 for opaque photos where banding is acceptable, or hardware bitmaps, or downsample to display size.
  3. Is there a hard limit on drawing size? → Yes, the render pipeline throws when a bitmap above about 100 MB is drawn (RecordingCanvas limit).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "bitmaps use a lot of memory, use Glide." Senior: does the math aloud, names the density trap, states the API-level storage change, and explains what image libraries do internally (sampling, pools, caches).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A banner PNG 1080x1920 placed in drawable-mdpi was decoded at 3x per axis on 99 devices of the test pool; 9x cost produced OOM only on high-density devices.

questions.promptHtml: Explain onTrimMemory levels. What should an app actually release at each level, and how is it different from onLowMemory?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Knowing the callback exists is junior. Knowing which resources to drop at which signal, and that the signal is advisory, is senior.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: onTrimMemory(level) is a ComponentCallbacks2 hint from the system that it wants processes to shed memory. TRIM_MEMORY_UI_HIDDEN (20) means my UI is no longer visible, so I drop view-related caches. The RUNNING_* levels (5, 10, 15) say I'm still in the foreground but the device is getting tight. The BACKGROUND/MODERATE/COMPLETE levels (40, 60, 80) say I'm cached and how close I am to being killed. It's advisory; LMK may kill me anyway. onLowMemory is the older coarse version, roughly the "complete" case.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Level Value Meaning Typical action
TRIM_MEMORY_RUNNING_MODERATE 5 foreground, system starting to get low trim non-essential caches
TRIM_MEMORY_RUNNING_LOW 10 foreground, low shrink image cache, stop prefetching
TRIM_MEMORY_RUNNING_CRITICAL 15 foreground, critical, background processes already being killed release almost everything non-visible
TRIM_MEMORY_UI_HIDDEN 20 all UI hidden drop UI-only resources (view caches, big bitmaps for screens)
TRIM_MEMORY_BACKGROUND 40 cached, near the start of LRU list release what is cheap to rebuild
TRIM_MEMORY_MODERATE 60 cached, middle of LRU list release more
TRIM_MEMORY_COMPLETE 80 cached, next kill candidate release everything rebuildable

Version note: several of these constants are marked deprecated in recent API levels (I recall the background-list ones around API 34 and the RUNNING_* ones around API 35, with the system no longer sending some of them). Verify on developer.android.com for the target API; TRIM_MEMORY_UI_HIDDEN remains the dependable, always-sent signal.

Where to receive it: Application, Activity, Service and ContentProvider implement ComponentCallbacks2. Anywhere else: context.registerComponentCallbacks(...). For caches, register once at app level so every cache hears it.

onLowMemory() predates it; it fires when the whole system is low, equivalent to asking for maximum release.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class App : Application() {
    override fun onTrimMemory(level: Int) {
        super.onTrimMemory(level)
        when {
            level >= ComponentCallbacks2.TRIM_MEMORY_COMPLETE -> ImageCache.clear()
            level >= ComponentCallbacks2.TRIM_MEMORY_BACKGROUND -> ImageCache.trimToSize(ImageCache.size() / 4)
            level >= ComponentCallbacks2.TRIM_MEMORY_UI_HIDDEN -> ImageCache.trimToSize(ImageCache.size() / 2)
        }
    }
}
# Test without waiting for real pressure
adb shell am send-trim-memory com.example.app RUNNING_CRITICAL
adb shell am send-trim-memory com.example.app BACKGROUND

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using level == X instead of >= on the numeric ordering when intending "at least this severe".
  • Doing heavy work (rebuilding caches) in the callback, which runs on the main thread.
  • Believing that releasing memory here prevents the kill. It only lowers the footprint, which may move you down the kill list.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why use UI_HIDDEN instead of onStop? → UI_HIDDEN triggers on the whole process's UI going away (all activities), while onStop is per-activity and fires during normal transitions between your own screens.
  2. Is it guaranteed to be delivered before a kill? → No. Kill can happen without any callback.
  3. How would you test the whole path? → am send-trim-memory, assert caches shrink, and verify via dumpsys meminfo before and after.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "release caches in onTrimMemory." Senior: ties levels to process state, avoids heavy work in the callback, notes deprecations, registers at app level, and tests it with adb.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A feed app released its decoded-bitmap cache on UI_HIDDEN and cut background kills of its process by about a quarter on 2 GB devices.

questions.promptHtml: In dumpsys meminfo, what do PSS, RSS, Private Dirty and USS mean, and which one do you trust to decide whether your app is "too big"?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Reading memory numbers wrongly leads to chasing noise. Shared pages make naive sums wrong.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: RSS counts every resident page the process maps, including pages shared with other processes, so it over-counts. PSS (proportional set size) divides shared pages among the processes that share them, so summing PSS across processes works. USS (unique set size) is only the private pages, which is what would be freed if the process died. For "how much does my app really cost", I use PSS for comparison and Private Dirty/USS for "what would a kill reclaim".

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Example. Process X has 100 MB of private pages and maps 60 MB of shared libraries that 3 processes (X, Y, Z) all use.

  • RSS(X) = 100 + 60 = 160 MB.
  • PSS(X) = 100 + 60/3 = 120 MB.
  • USS(X) = 100 MB. Sum of PSS across X, Y, Z gives total physical use without double counting; sum of RSS would count the 60 MB shared three times.

meminfo columns:

  • Pss Total: proportional.
  • Private Dirty: private pages that were modified; cannot be dropped without swapping or killing (Android has no regular disk swap; zRAM compresses instead).
  • Private Clean: unmodified private pages (like file-backed code), can be dropped and re-read.
  • Swap PSS: portion compressed into zRAM.

LMK decides on its own pressure heuristics, but practically the data that hurts you is Private Dirty (anon + dirty) because it can't be reclaimed cheaply.

           Process X
 [ private dirty 100 MB ][ shared libs 60 MB, shared by X,Y,Z ]
 RSS = 160   PSS = 120   USS = 100

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
adb shell dumpsys meminfo com.example.app            # summary + PSS per category
adb shell dumpsys meminfo -a com.example.app         # full, includes "Dalvik Other", "Ashmem"
adb shell cat /proc/$(adb shell pidof com.example.app)/smaps_rollup   # RSS, PSS, Private_Dirty rollup

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Comparing RSS before and after a fix and calling it a win while PSS is unchanged.
  • Measuring right after launch. Do a few GC cycles and a stable state; use System.gc() is not reliable, use profiler "force GC" for comparison.
  • Reading "TOTAL" of one category as the app's total.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does the Android Studio profiler show a smaller number than meminfo TOTAL? → The profiler's memory graph categories are subsets (Java, Native, Graphics, Stack, Code, Others); totals use PSS and exclude some system-attributed shared memory.
  2. Does a bigger PSS mean the LMK kills it first? → Not alone. Oom adj (process importance) is first; PSS breaks ties among similar adj.
  3. What is zRAM's role? → Compressed in-RAM swap. Swap PSS shows pages sitting in it; touching them costs CPU to decompress.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "PSS is memory used by the app." Senior: gives the proportional math, uses Private Dirty as the reclaimable-by-kill number, and avoids RSS summation.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An SDK team claimed "no memory cost" by showing RSS stayed flat; PSS and Private Dirty showed +40 MB because new anonymous pages replaced already-shared ones.

questions.promptHtml: How does garbage collection work on modern Android (ART)? What do the GC lines in logcat tell you, and when does GC actually hurt the UI?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks that you can reason about GC as a cost model instead of "GC is automatic, not my problem".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: ART uses a mostly concurrent, compacting collector (concurrent copying since Android 8.0) that does most work on a background thread with very short pauses. GC hurts when I allocate faster than it reclaims. Then an allocation can block waiting for a GC ("GC_FOR_ALLOC"), or the GC thread steals CPU from the render path. I read the art log lines for cause, freed amount, heap utilization, and pause time to see which case I'm in.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Reachability model: objects reachable from GC roots (static fields, thread stacks, JNI references, class loaders) survive; everything else is garbage. No reference counting.
  • Collectors over history: Dalvik mark-sweep (stop-the-world, tens of ms pauses) → ART CMS (Android 5 to 7) → Concurrent Copying (CC) default from Android 8.0 (API 26). Newer releases add other collectors; see the ART internals question.
  • GC causes seen in logs: Alloc / GC_FOR_ALLOC (an allocation failed, so the allocating thread waits; the bad one), Background / Concurrent (heap crossed a threshold, GC runs on a daemon thread), Explicit (System.gc()), NativeAlloc (native allocation pressure, e.g., bitmaps), CollectorTransition, HeapTrim.
  • Typical line (format varies by release):
I/art: Background concurrent copying GC freed 41230(2MB) AllocSpace objects, 3(1MB) LOS objects,
       36% free, 38MB/60MB, paused 215us,402us total 61.2ms
I/art: Waiting for a blocking GC Alloc          <-- allocation had to wait: a red flag
I/art: Alloc concurrent copying GC freed ... paused 1.2ms total 48ms   <-- blocking GC on alloc
  • Reading it: "freed X(bytes) objects" = churn; "% free, used/total" = headroom (near the cap means pressure); "paused" = stop-the-world portions; "total" = wall-clock concurrent time.
  • Why GC jank is not about pauses anymore: pauses are typically sub-millisecond to a few ms. The visible cost is (1) blocking GC during allocation near the cap and (2) CPU contention on small cores while rendering at 60/90/120 Hz.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
adb logcat -s art:I dalvikvm:I              # GC lines
adb shell am dumpheap com.example.app /data/local/tmp/x.hprof
adb shell dumpsys meminfo com.example.app   # includes "Objects", "Views", "Activities" counts
// Cheap runtime signals
val rt = Runtime.getRuntime()
Log.d("GC", "used=${(rt.totalMemory() - rt.freeMemory()) shr 20}MB max=${rt.maxMemory() shr 20}MB")
Log.d("GC", "gcCount=${Debug.getRuntimeStat("art.gc.gc-count")} blocked=${Debug.getRuntimeStat("art.gc.blocking-gc-count")}")

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Calling System.gc() to "free memory". It triggers an explicit full collection and does not fix leaks.
  • Believing finalizers or WeakReference give predictable cleanup timing.
  • Assuming "no GC pauses in logs" means no GC jank; check allocation stalls and CPU.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is a GC root? → Static fields, live thread stack locals, JNI global/local refs, class loader and system roots.
  2. Why do Dalvik-era GC tips (pooling everything) mostly not apply now? → Concurrent compaction made pauses tiny, so pool only hot, large, or churny objects.
  3. How do you see blocking GCs in production? → Debug.getRuntimeStat("art.gc.blocking-gc-count") and blocking-gc-time (API 23+) reported to telemetry.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "GC frees unused objects; avoid creating objects in loops." Senior: names the collector, distinguishes blocking vs background GC, reads the log line, and measures with runtime stats instead of guessing.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A chat list hit 1.5 s jank bursts on mid devices; logs showed repeated Alloc GCs at 95% heap use caused by a 40 MB cache plus a leak, not by "slow rendering".

questions.promptHtml: What is allocation churn, why does it cause jank even though the heap is not leaking, and what are the most common hidden allocations in Kotlin Android code?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Production perf bugs are often churn, not leaks. Probes knowledge of Kotlin boxing, lambdas, and per-frame code.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Churn is creating many short-lived objects rapidly. Nothing leaks, but the heap fills quickly, GC runs often, and on a busy main thread or a small CPU it competes with frame work. Hot paths such as onDraw, onBindViewHolder, scroll listeners, and per-item mapping are where it bites. Typical hidden allocators: boxing primitives in generic collections, string formatting and concatenation, capturing lambdas, Regex constructed in a loop, Paint/Rect created inside onDraw, and chained map/filter creating intermediate lists.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Budget example. A RecyclerView binding at 60 fps while flinging binds about 6 rows per frame in the worst case. If each bind allocates a formatted String (60 B), a SimpleDateFormat (about 1 KB internal state, not cheap), and 5 lambdas (about 24 B each), that is about 1.2 KB per row, 7.2 KB per frame, 430 KB/s. Small alone, but with a 20 MB young-ish headroom it triggers a collection every ~45 s of scroll plus bigger spikes when parsing happens. Add the SimpleDateFormat fix and it falls below 100 KB/s. The principle: find the top allocators, not guess.

Hidden allocators in Kotlin:

  • List<Int>, Map<Long, X>, Array<Int?>: each element boxed (Java Integer cache only covers -128..127).
  • Non-inline lambdas that capture variables allocate a closure object per call; inline functions avoid it.
  • "$a $b" builds a StringBuilder + String each time.
  • for (i in 0 until n) is optimized, but forEach on non-inline collections or .withIndex() may allocate iterators/pairs depending on form.
  • Regex("..."), Pattern.compile, DateTimeFormatter, Gson(), SimpleDateFormat: expensive to construct, cache them.
  • Defensive copies: list.toList(), copy() of big data classes in state reducers.

How to find them: Android Studio Memory Profiler "Record Java/Kotlin allocations" (sampled), or Perfetto Java heap sampling, and compare allocation count per frame.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// BAD: allocates a Paint and Rect every frame
override fun onDraw(c: Canvas) {
    val p = Paint(Paint.ANTI_ALIAS_FLAG).apply { color = Color.RED }
    val r = Rect(0, 0, width, height)
    c.drawRect(r, p)
}

// GOOD: hoist, mutate in place
private val paint = Paint(Paint.ANTI_ALIAS_FLAG).apply { color = Color.RED }
private val rect = Rect()
override fun onDraw(c: Canvas) {
    rect.set(0, 0, width, height)
    c.drawRect(rect, paint)
}
// Primitive-specialized collections avoid boxing
val counts = androidx.collection.MutableIntIntMap()  // or SparseIntArray / LongSparseArray

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Pooling everything. A pool of trivially small objects costs more complexity than the GC does.
  • Optimizing without a profile. Allocation is cheap in ART; only hot paths matter.
  • Moving allocations to a background thread and calling it fixed. Total GC pressure is the same.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is Paint allocation in onDraw flagged by tools? → Android Lint warns (DrawAllocation).
  2. When is an object pool correct? → Large (bitmaps, big buffers), expensive to build, or in a measured hot loop.
  3. How do you prove improvement? → Allocation count and GC count/time per scenario run before and after, with a macrobenchmark or a repeatable scripted flow.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "avoid creating objects in onDraw." Senior: quantifies, lists Kotlin-specific hidden allocations, uses sampling tools, and warns against premature pooling.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A search screen allocating a Regex per keystroke per item (60 items) produced bursty GCs and visible typing lag on 3 GB devices.

questions.promptHtml: How does Android decide which process to kill under memory pressure, and how can you tell in production that your app was killed for memory rather than crashing?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: LMK kills leave no crash trace. Senior candidates know how to detect them.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Android keeps a score per process (oom_score_adj) that reflects importance: the foreground app is 0, visible about 100, perceptible about 200, services around 500, and cached processes 900+. The userspace daemon lmkd watches memory pressure (PSI based on devices with kernel support, older versions used free-memory thresholds) and kills the highest score first, which means cached background apps die first. A kill is a SIGKILL, so no exception or onDestroy. In production I use ApplicationExitInfo (API 30+) and look for REASON_LOW_MEMORY.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
